tagline: Turn your cooking skills into online income — without opening a restaurant.

tasks: Film and post your first 30-second cooking video on TikTok
Create a Facebook page for your food content or food business
Study 3 viral Filipino food TikToks and note their format

summary.description: You don't need a culinary degree or a commercial kitchen. Filipinos who can cook well are earning online through food content, recipe blogs, online food selling, and cooking tutorials. The key is combining your cooking skill with one digital skill — video, writing, or social media.
who_is_this_for: Home cooks who get compliments on their food
Stay-at-home parents who already cook daily
People interested in food content creation

reality_check.honest_assessment: Cooking alone won't pay you online. You need to pair it with content creation (TikTok/YouTube), food selling (GrabFood/Facebook), or recipe writing. Your first month will likely earn ₱0–₱3,000. The fastest path is food content on TikTok — you can monetize through brand deals at 10K+ followers. Food selling earns faster but requires capital and logistics.
reality_check.what_beginners_underestimate: How much content you need to post before anything goes viral. Expect to post 30–50 videos before one gets real traction. Also, food selling has hidden costs — packaging, delivery, and ingredient waste add up fast.
reality_check.why_people_fail: They post 5 videos, get 50 views each, and quit. Or they start a food business without calculating costs and end up losing money. Or they try both content and selling at the same time and do neither well.
reality_check.how_to_avoid_failure: Pick ONE path — content or selling — and commit to it for 30 days straight. For content, post daily. For selling, start with just 2–3 menu items. Track every peso spent and earned from day one.

roadmap.title: Choose Your Path
roadmap.why: Cooking can earn money in very different ways. Picking one path early prevents you from spreading yourself thin and quitting from overwhelm.

steps.action: Decide: content creator or food seller
steps.detail: Content = TikTok/YouTube cooking videos. Selling = home-based food business via Facebook/GrabFood. Pick one to start. You can add the other later.
steps.outcome: You have a clear direction and can focus all your energy on one path.

steps.detail: For content: create a TikTok account focused on cooking. For selling: create a Facebook page with your menu, prices, and delivery area.
steps.outcome: Your platform is live and ready for your first post or menu listing.

steps.detail: Watch how they shoot, what angles they use, how short their videos are. Copy the format, not the recipes.
steps.outcome: You understand the format that works and can replicate it with your own recipes.

roadmap.milestone: Platform chosen and account set up

roadmap.title: Create Your First Content or Product
roadmap.why: Nothing happens until you publish. Your first 10 posts teach you more than any tutorial — and they give the algorithm data to work with.

steps.action: Post 10 cooking videos or list 5 menu items
steps.detail: For content: film 10 short recipe videos (30–60 seconds). For selling: photograph 5 dishes with prices and post on your Facebook page.
steps.outcome: You have real content or products online that people can find, share, and buy.

steps.action: Use natural lighting and a clean background
steps.detail: You don't need equipment. A window and a white plate make food look professional. Shoot during daytime.
steps.outcome: Your food photos and videos look clean and appetizing without spending on gear.

steps.detail: Post your videos or menu in community groups, food groups, and buy-and-sell groups in your area.
steps.outcome: You get your first views, comments, and potentially your first customers from your own community.

roadmap.milestone: First 10 posts published or first 5 orders received

roadmap.title: Build an Audience or Customer Base
roadmap.why: One-time views don't pay the bills. Repeat followers and repeat customers create the foundation for real income.

steps.action: Post consistently — 1 video or menu update per day
steps.detail: Algorithms reward consistency. TikTok promotes daily posters. Food customers return to pages that update regularly.
steps.outcome: The algorithm starts pushing your content to more people, and customers check your page regularly.

steps.detail: Reply to every comment within 1 hour. Ask questions back: 'What recipe should I try next?' Engagement boosts reach.
steps.outcome: Your engagement rate increases, which triggers more algorithmic reach and builds community trust.

steps.action: Start a recipe blog on Medium or WordPress
steps.detail: Write 5 recipes with photos. Add affiliate links to kitchen tools. This creates passive income alongside your main path.
steps.outcome: You have a second income stream through affiliate commissions and a written portfolio of your recipes.
resources: How to write a recipe blog post

roadmap.title: Monetize
roadmap.why: An audience without monetization is a hobby. This phase turns your following or customer base into predictable income.

steps.action: For content: pitch local food brands for sponsorships
steps.detail: At 5K+ followers, message brands: 'I'll feature your product in a cooking video for ₱1,000–₱3,000.' Start with local sauces, condiments, or kitchen tools.
steps.outcome: You earn per video from brand deals, turning content creation into a real income source.

steps.action: For selling: join GrabFood or Foodpanda
steps.detail: Expand beyond Facebook orders. Platform delivery increases volume. Register your home kitchen with your local LGU if required.
steps.outcome: You reach customers outside your immediate network, significantly increasing daily orders.

steps.detail: Compile your best 20 recipes into a PDF. Sell it for ₱99–₱199 on Gumroad. Use your TikTok or Facebook audience to promote it.
steps.outcome: You have a passive income product that earns while you sleep — every new follower is a potential buyer.
resources: How to create a PDF ebook

income_paths.title: Food Content Creation
income_paths.detail: Create cooking videos on TikTok, YouTube, or Instagram Reels. Earn from brand sponsorships, affiliate links, and platform monetization.
income_paths.best_for: People who enjoy being on camera (or showing their hands) and can post consistently every day
income_paths.typical_beginner_mistake: Focusing on production quality instead of volume — your first 20 videos should be fast and imperfect, not polished

income_paths.title: Home-Based Food Selling
income_paths.detail: Sell home-cooked meals, baked goods, or meal prep packages via Facebook, GrabFood, or direct delivery in your area.
income_paths.best_for: People who prefer tangible work and already cook daily — this monetizes what you're already doing
income_paths.typical_beginner_mistake: Not tracking ingredient costs and thinking all revenue is profit — always calculate cost per serving before setting prices

income_paths.title: Recipe Writing & Blogging
income_paths.detail: Write recipes for food blogs, content sites, or your own blog with ad revenue and affiliate links to kitchen products.
income_paths.best_for: People who enjoy writing and photography — this is the slowest path but builds long-term passive income
income_paths.typical_beginner_mistake: Writing recipes without SEO — nobody will find your recipe if you don't target what people actually search for

income_paths.title: Digital Recipe Products
income_paths.detail: Create and sell recipe eBooks, meal plan PDFs, or cooking guides on Gumroad or your own site.
income_paths.best_for: People who already have an audience (even small) and want to create something once and sell it repeatedly
income_paths.typical_beginner_mistake: Creating the product before building an audience — you need people to sell to first

platforms.name: TikTok
platforms.why: Fastest way to build a food audience. Short recipe videos can go viral even with zero followers.

platforms.name: Facebook
platforms.why: Best for local food selling. Create a page, join community groups, and take orders directly via Messenger.

platforms.name: GrabFood
platforms.why: Expand your delivery range beyond personal contacts. Requires registration but significantly increases order volume.

platforms.name: Gumroad
platforms.why: Sell digital recipe books and meal plans. No upfront cost. GCash-compatible via PayPal.

tools.name: CapCut
tools.purpose: Edit cooking videos for TikTok and Reels. Free, mobile-friendly, and has food-specific templates.
tools.why_it_matters: Raw footage looks amateur. Even 5 minutes of editing — cuts, music, text overlay — makes your food content look professional and shareable.
tools.when_to_start: Day 1 — before posting your first video

tools.name: Canva
tools.purpose: Create recipe cards, menu designs, and food business branding.
tools.why_it_matters: A clean menu or recipe card makes your food business look legitimate. Clients and followers trust polished presentation.
tools.when_to_start: Week 2 — after you've decided your path and need branding

tools.name: Google Docs
tools.purpose: Write and organize recipes before turning them into content or products.
tools.why_it_matters: Keeping recipes organized saves you from re-inventing every time you post. It also becomes the raw material for your recipe eBook.
tools.when_to_start: Day 1 — start documenting your recipes immediately

tools.name: Snapseed
tools.purpose: Edit food photos on your phone. Adjust brightness and contrast to make dishes look appetizing.
tools.why_it_matters: Food photos with proper lighting and color correction get 2–3x more engagement than dark, unedited shots.
tools.when_to_start: Week 1 — use it for your food selling photos or blog posts

faq.question: Do I need a commercial kitchen to sell food online?
faq.answer: For small-scale Facebook selling, most Filipinos start from their home kitchen. If you scale to GrabFood or Foodpanda, check your local LGU requirements — some require basic food safety permits.

faq.question: Can I earn from cooking without showing my face?
faq.answer: Yes. Many viral food TikToks show only hands and ingredients. Overhead shots of cooking are the most popular format — no face needed.

faq.question: How much capital do I need to start selling food?
faq.answer: For content creation: almost zero — just your phone and ingredients you already have. For food selling: ₱1,000–₱3,000 for initial ingredients and packaging materials.

faq.question: What type of food content performs best?
faq.answer: Budget meals ('₱50 ulam'), quick recipes (under 60 seconds), and Filipino comfort food consistently get the most views. Trendy recipes also work but have shorter viral windows.

faq.question: Can I do both content creation and food selling?
faq.answer: Yes, and they complement each other. Your TikTok cooking videos drive customers to your food business, and your food business gives you content to post.
